name: Xhosa kingdom
summary: Xhosa chiefdoms of the Eastern Cape, which fought nine frontier wars against Cape settlers and Britain (1779–1879) and suffered the cattle-killing famine of 1856–57.

location.value: The Eastern Cape; the page names the Kei and Fish rivers and the Amatola and Winterberg mountains, and says Xhosa have lived in the area since the 7th century. The Mbashe is not named.

terrain.value: Rolling grassland, river valleys and coastal hills.

climate.value: Mild, with summer rains; droughts in some years.

resources.value: Cattle and grazing land, fields for sorghum and maize.

disasters.value: The cattle-killing movement of 1856–57 led to the slaughter of about 400,000 cattle and a famine that killed tens of thousands.

population.value: Over ten million Xhosa speakers today per the text, 9,660,004 in the infobox (South Africa 9,415,133 in 2022; Eastern Cape 5,102,053). These are modern figures, not kingdom-era ones.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal or market town.

migration.value: Pushed east by Cape settlers after each frontier war; after the cattle-killing many went to work in the Cape Colony.

economicBase.value: Cattle were the basis of wealth in the river basins' rich farming and grazing land. Sorghum appears only as a food.

tradeRoutes.value: Traded cattle, ivory and hides with the Cape Colony for beads, metal and later guns.

wealth.value: Wealth and status were measured in cattle.

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute, cloth, cowries and trade goods.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above farmers; captives and slaves at the bottom.

governmentType.value: The page does not describe the Gcaleka and Rharhabe lines; oral tradition says the kingdom was founded before the 1400s, when Tshawe brought independent Nguni clans together.

keyRulers.value: The page does not name Hintsa, Sarhili, Ngqika or Sandile; they need another source.
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Xhosa people (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Cape Frontier Wars (checked 15 Nov 2026) (Britannica names Hintsa (shot in British custody in 1834–35) and Sandile (deposed in 1851); Sarhili and Maqoma are not mentioned)

succession.value: The heir was the son of the chief’s “great wife”; other sons founded their own chiefdoms.

institutions.value: Chiefs ruled with councils of advisers; courts settled disputes over cattle and land.

stability.value: A century of frontier wars with the Cape Colony and splits between chiefdoms.

eliteConflict.value: The Gcaleka and Rharhabe branches split under King Phalo’s sons (1700s) and often competed.

armyAndTech.value: Warriors with spears and shields, later firearms; mobile raids suited to bush country.

majorWars.value: The Cape Frontier Wars are called some of the longest military resistance to colonialism; the page gives no number or dates for them.
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Xhosa people (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Cape Frontier Wars (checked 15 Nov 2026) (about 100 years of intermittent war from 1779; the early-1850s war is called the eighth and most costly)

territoryChange.value: Lost land step by step to the Cape Colony; British Kaffraria (1847) and the Transkei (1879–94) were annexed.

alliancesRivals.value: Fought the British and Boer settlers; neighbours and sometimes rivals were the Thembu, Mpondo and Mfengu.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Open to trade and, slowly, to missionaries and mission schools such as Lovedale (1841).

communicationTransport.value: Footpaths and cattle tracks; messengers carried news between chiefs.

religion.value: The infobox lists uThixo, Qamata and Christianity, and rituals honour the ancestors. Missions of the 1820s are not on the page.

languageWriting.value: isiXhosa, a Bantu language with click sounds from Khoekhoe; missionaries first wrote it down in the 1820s.

artsArchitecture.value: Beadwork, praise poetry (izibongo) and round thatched houses in homesteads.

socialStructure.value: Chiefs and councillors, heads of homesteads, wives, young men and herd boys.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the royal lineage and shared Xhosa customs such as initiation.

dailyLife.value: Village farming; cassava, millet or sorghum.

neighbours.value: The Cape Colony, the Thembu and Mpondo kingdoms, the Khoekhoe and the Mfengu.

ideasReligions.value: Prophets such as Nxele (1819) and Nongqawuse (1856) blended Christian and traditional ideas.

colonisation.value: British annexation, completed when the Transkei was taken over (1879–94).

riseSignals.value: Oral tradition says the Xhosa Kingdom was founded before the 15th century by Tshawe, who overthrew his brother Cirha; the Xhosa descend from Nguni clans and the area has been inhabited since the 7th century. The entry’s start year of 1600 is later than this tradition.

peakPeriod.value: The page gives no peak or territorial figures for the 1700s.

declineSignals.value: The cattle-killing of 1856–57 broke Xhosa independence.

outcome.value: The cattle-killing movement of 1856–1858, a millennialist response to cattle lung disease and loss of land and autonomy, was followed by famine and political division. The page does not date the end of the kingdom. Britannica dates the mass cattle killing to 1857.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Xhosa people (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Cape Frontier Wars (checked 15 Nov 2026) (it says the movement ended Xhosa military resistance for about two decades)

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
